analysis.one_liner: Strips legal immunity from websites that fail to act on deepfakes and cyberstalking.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 1, 2025 with one Republican cosponsor and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite Section 230, the law that currently shields websites from lawsuits over what users post. Websites would lose that protection unless they run a reasonable process to prevent and remove cyberstalking and nonconsensual intimate images, including sexual deepfakes, and must take down reported content within 48 hours. It would also tighten the TAKE IT DOWN Act, the existing law on nonconsensual intimate images, so that realistic AI-generated forgeries are treated the same as real photos, and would count AI-generated content as platform-created content. The Federal Trade Commission would write rules to carry this out within 180 days of enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of cyberstalking and of nonconsensual intimate images — including realistic AI-generated 'deepfake' pornography — who would gain a fast, standardized removal process and a way to sue platforms that ignore them.

how_it_helps.text: Websites open to the public would lose Section 230 legal immunity unless they implement a reasonable process covering prevention, notice-and-removal, data preservation for legal proceedings, and removal of court-determined unlawful content [S2].
Platforms would have to remove reported intimate privacy violations and cyberstalking content within 48 hours and make reasonable efforts to remove identical copies [S2].

The bill would amend the TAKE IT DOWN Act so 'sexually explicit digital forgery' explicitly covers depictions made or manipulated to be virtually indistinguishable from authentic images, and would remove an existing exception [S2].

It would expand the definition of who 'creates or develops' content to include use of a generative model, meaning AI tools used to generate unlawful content could count as platform-created content rather than user content [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly accessible websites and apps — chiefly social media platforms — which would lose their Section 230 shield, face 48-hour removal deadlines, compliance costs, and litigation risk if their processes fall short; AI model developers would face new exposure under the expanded content-creation definition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media platforms and AI developers

drawbacks.text: A good-faith objection: carving cyberstalking and intimate privacy violations out of Section 230 could push platforms to remove lawful content to avoid lawsuits, since the 48-hour clock starts on any facially valid request and the bill acknowledges First Amendment concerns but does not resolve them [S2].
Compliance costs and litigation exposure would fall hardest on smaller sites and apps, which have fewer staff than major platforms and could struggle to meet the same process requirements [S2].

The bill lets the FCC add 'any other process or requirement determined necessary,' and requires FTC rulemaking within 180 days, so the final scope of platform duties would be set by regulators rather than by the statute's text alone [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims of nonconsensual intimate images and stalking, the bill addresses a real, documented harm and would give them leverage they largely lack today. The honest cost is the risk of over-removal of lawful speech and heavier compliance burdens that weigh most on small platforms. How well it balances depends on regulations that do not yet exist, so the trade-off cannot be fully judged from the bill text alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 1, 2025 by Rep. Jake Auchincloss with one Republican cosponsor and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the action history [S4].
The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill could still move, but it currently sits at the first procedural step [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet; platforms keep the Section 230 shield as it stands while the bill waits in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are from opposite parties — a Democrat and one Republican — and no member or group is recorded opposing the bill, because it has not yet been considered.

industries.note: Platforms would lose their Section 230 immunity unless they actively police cyberstalking and nonconsensual intimate images on 48-hour removal deadlines, raising compliance and litigation costs. Those costs exist because the platforms profit from hosting user content while victims currently have little recourse.

By expanding 'creation or development' to include use of a generative model, the bill could expose AI toolmakers to liability when their models produce unlawful intimate forgeries. Consumers harmed by deepfakes currently have few effective remedies against the output of these tools.

industries.industry: Broadband, email, messaging, and data storage services
industries.note: These services are expressly excluded from the 'covered platform' definition, so they avoid the new duties while competitors face them — though their gain is mainly relative, since they were never the target.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with two sponsors that are referred to a committee and see no action in their first weeks usually die quietly at the end of the Congress. Committee consideration, a hearing, or a markup would have to be scheduled before any floor vote, and there is no sign of that yet.
